column4: The section explicitly uses this verse: God completes His favor upon the Prophet and guides him on a straight path, joining completed ni'mah to the requested path.
The clear victory granted here is the opening gift whose next ayah names completed favor and straight-path guidance.
The section explicitly pairs this qiblah verse with 48:2: completing God's favor upon the community is stated together with their being guided.
God's completion of the religion and completion of His favor are one declaration here, giving the section's "completed favor" its communal, religious form.
Purification is followed by God's completing His favor so that people may be grateful; it makes a response of thanks part of received completion.
The verse explicitly says that God will complete His favor on Joseph and the family of Jacob, showing the section's favor as a gift extended across a household.
Shelter, clothing, and protection culminate in God completing His favor so that the recipients submit; provision reaches a completed response.
Completing the counted days is joined to magnifying God for His guidance and being grateful, a ritual-scale parallel to completed favor and praise.
Abraham is grateful for God's favors, then chosen and guided to a straight path; this is the section's gratitude-before-guidance sequence in one ayah.
Those who obey God and the Messenger are placed with those whom God has favored, directly expanding Fatiha's favored people into a guided company.
The garden-dwellers praise God for having guided them there and say they could not have been guided without Him, completing the section's path-to-hamd image.
God guides believers into gardens; this arrival supplies the guided destination whose inhabitants voice praise in 10:10.
The residents' final call is praise to God, Lord of the worlds; after 10:9's guidance into the garden, Fatiha's opening hamd is heard as the road's end.
People are told to rejoice in God's bounty and mercy rather than what they accumulate, directing joy away from possessive self-credit toward the giver.
God's finding the Prophet an orphan and giving shelter begins the concrete favors whose public acknowledgment concludes in 93:11.
God's finding the Prophet in need of guidance and guiding him makes this surah a direct neighboring instance of the section's favor-as-path.
God's finding the Prophet in need and enriching him gives the material favor that is to be acknowledged, not claimed.
Because the Prophet was sheltered as an orphan in 93:6, he is told not to oppress the orphan; received care passes toward another vulnerable person.
The command not to repel the petitioner continues the surah's conversion of received abundance into a humane answer.
The command to speak of the favor of one's Lord is the section's public telling of received good, sharply unlike using a gift to reproach another.
Worship of the Lord of this House is the response the section identifies as due to a completed, received favor.
The Lord fed Quraysh against hunger and secured them against fear, providing the concrete favor that grounds 106:3's worship.
David and Solomon answer their granted knowledge by saying praise belongs to God who favored them; it is an enacted, non-boastful hamd for a gift.
Solomon asks to be enabled to thank for God's favor upon him and his parents and to do righteous work, carrying received favor into grateful action.
When the throne arrives, Solomon calls it bounty from his Lord and a test of whether he will thank or be ungrateful, making the recipient's answer explicit.
The Lord is said to possess bounty toward people while most do not give thanks, stating the giver and the failed response in one line.
The child asks to be enabled to thank for the favor bestowed on him and his parents and to do good, linking inherited favor to an ethical return.
The section's named dictionary sense of en'ame as giving more and increasing is enacted here: gratitude is answered with increase.
One who has received what God gave is told to do good as God did good to him; the section's hand-to-hand movement of goodness becomes an ethic.
Out of mercy God makes night and day for rest and seeking bounty so that people may give thanks, turning the daily cycle into provision and response.
Those given good provisions are commanded to eat and give thanks to God, a direct provision-to-response scene.
God gives people what they ask and says His favors cannot be counted; the impossibility of exhausting them deepens the section's call to name the Giver's goodness.
The inability to enumerate God's favor, followed by His forgiveness and mercy, gives the section's praise a merciful source beyond any complete human inventory.
Every favor people possess is from God; the ayah establishes the giver in the section's scene before the recipient praises or denies.
Eating lawful provision is explicitly followed by thanking God for His favor, binding material reception to worshipful acknowledgment.
God has lavished outward and inward blessings on people; its visible-and-hidden scope enlarges the section's single handed-over favor.
The House of David is commanded to work in gratitude after its extraordinary provisions, making gratitude active rather than merely verbal.
Saba is told to eat its Lord's provision and thank Him; a fertile place and a forgiving Lord form a concrete gift-and-response scene.
The command to remember God's favor is immediately tied to His unique provision from heaven and earth, locating every received good with its giver.
People eat fruit their own hands did not make and are asked why they do not give thanks, directly confronting the receiver of unearned provision.
Cattle furnish benefits and drink, followed by the question whether people will be grateful; it restages favor and answer through a daily provision.
The sacrificial animals are made subject so that people magnify God for guiding them; a provided means is returned as public exaltation.
After being saved in the Ark, Noah is commanded to say praise belongs to God who rescued them, a spoken answer to deliverance.
The succession of night and day is made for one who wants to remember or be grateful, presenting time itself as a recurring favor that solicits response.
Abraham's public account of his Lord begins with creation and guidance, making guidance a named good rather than an achievement he claims.
Abraham names the Lord who feeds and gives him drink, a concise instance of telling the Giver's concrete benefits.
Abraham attributes healing in sickness to his Lord, extending the section's catalogued goodness beyond food and wealth.
Abraham attributes death and renewed life to his Lord, keeping ultimate life within the same grateful account of divine action.
Abraham hopes that his Lord will forgive him on Judgment Day; mercy and forgiveness complete his spoken account of the Giver.
Winds bring good news, let people taste mercy, move ships to seek bounty, and are said to invite gratitude; the ayah stages gift, livelihood, and response together.
The dwellers say praise to God for removing sorrow; 35:35 identifies their permanent dwelling as a gift of His bounty.
God settled them in the lasting home out of His bounty, supplying the received favor for 35:34's praise.
God gives believers their rewards in full and increases them from His bounty, closely matching the section's dictionary sense of doing a good fully and adding more.
The garden-dwellers praise God because He fulfilled His promise and gave them the land, a second end-of-the-road return to hamd.
God made night for rest and day for sight and is full of bounty toward people, yet most do not thank; this directly tests the section's expected answer.
The sea is subjected so people seek God's bounty and may give thanks, coupling a usable gift with the purpose of gratitude.
Lot's rescue is called a favor from God and is explicitly said to be how He rewards one who is grateful.
After the earth's fruits, grain, and fragrant plants, the refrain asks which favors of the Lord can be denied; provision demands acknowledgment.
After human and jinn creation, the refrain makes created life itself one of the Lord's favors that cannot rightly be denied.
After naming the Lord of the two easts and two wests, the refrain makes the ordered horizons part of the favor-and-recognition scene.
The refrain follows the meeting seas held apart by a barrier, asking the two kinds to answer that ordered mercy without denial.
Pearls and coral emerging from the two seas precede the refrain, making their yielded beauty a concrete favor to acknowledge.
The ships like mountains in the sea precede the refrain, extending the section's guided journey image to a traveled, God-enabled route.
After all creatures perish while the majestic Lord remains, the refrain asks about denied favors at the boundary between passing creatures and their enduring Lord.
All in heavens and earth ask of God and He is each day upon a matter; the refrain makes ongoing dependence a favor that cannot be claimed as one's own.
After the two accountable kinds are told that they will be attended to, the refrain turns the question of denied favors into a boundary of accountability.
The refrain follows the challenge that humans and jinn cannot pass the realms without authority, framing creaturely limit against the Lord's favors.
After the threat of flame and molten copper, the refrain brings denial of the Lord's favors into a judgment scene rather than a scene of private possession.
The sky splitting and becoming red precedes the refrain; cosmic upheaval gives the favor-question a stark eschatological boundary.
After the statement that neither human nor jinn will be questioned about sin at that point, the refrain joins denied favors to irrevocable judgment.
Criminals recognized by their marks precede the refrain, making the refusal to acknowledge the Lord's favors answerable in the scene of seizure.
The refrain follows the depiction of Hell and boiling water, setting denial of divine favor against its ultimate contrary.
The one who fears standing before his Lord receives two gardens; the refrain makes the promised gardens favors to recognize rather than status to boast of.
The two branching gardens precede the refrain, giving a particular garden image to the question of denied favors.
The two flowing springs are followed by the refrain, making freely running water a named scene of provision and acknowledgment.
Every pair of fruit in the gardens precedes the refrain; abundance here is explicitly placed before the question of denial.
Reclining amid near fruit precedes the refrain, presenting received ease without any self-credit by its recipients.
The refrain follows the garden companions described as untouched, making even intimate garden joy part of the Lord's acknowledged favor.
Their likeness to rubies and coral precedes the refrain, returning beauty to the same sea-and-garden field of given favors.
After the axiom that goodness is repaid only with goodness, the refrain asks about denied favors; it meets the section's question of how good should answer good.
Two further gardens are named before the refrain, extending the plural gifts given to the one who rightly fears the Lord.
The dark-green gardens precede the refrain, making luxuriant renewal another explicit favor rather than a possession claimed by its inhabitant.
Two gushing springs precede the refrain, repeating water as a supplied gift whose source the recipient must not deny.
Fruit, dates, and pomegranates precede the refrain, keeping food in the section's giver-to-recipient scene.
Good and beautiful companions precede the refrain, placing delight within the same repeated call to acknowledge the Lord's favors.
Sheltered companions in pavilions precede the refrain, naming protected joy as a favor rather than a human accomplishment.
Their untouched state precedes the refrain, giving the question of denied favors a particular garden detail without conflating it with another ayah.
Green cushions and fine carpets precede the final refrain, so the section's praise of the giver reaches the last scene of garden repose.
The gift of abundance is followed in the next ayah by worship and sacrifice, making divine giving the ground of ritual response.
The command to pray to the Lord and sacrifice is the response to the abundance granted in 108:1, not a self-advertisement of it.
God's help and victory provide the completed gift whose response is ordered in 110:3, echoing the section's use of a clear victory before praise.
After help and victory, the Prophet is commanded to glorify with his Lord's praise and seek forgiveness; success returns as hamd rather than boast.
God changes former enemies into brothers and saves them from the Fire; the command to remember this favor makes communal reconciliation a received gift.
Sending a messenger who recites, purifies, and teaches is called God's favor upon believers, joining favor to guided formation.
Believers are reminded that they too were once in the other's position before God favored them; received grace is made grounds for careful treatment of others.
Moses tells his people to remember God's favor: prophets, kingship, and gifts not given to others. It makes favor corporate and historical.
God tells Jesus to remember His favor upon him and his mother, showing favor named to its recipient without the recipient turning it into a claim over others.
After establishing people on earth and providing livelihoods, God notes how little they give thanks, a broad earthly version of the section's scene.
The weak community is sheltered, strengthened, and provided good things so it may be grateful; every stage is a concrete received benefit.
Joseph calls God's favor upon his family and all people while noting that most do not give thanks, pairing favor with its missing response.
After reunion, Joseph tells his family that his Lord has been good to him through rescue and reconciliation, publicly recounting benefits without reproaching anyone.
Moses tells Israel to remember God's favor when He saved them from Pharaoh's people, giving the section a communal rescue behind gratitude.
Abraham praises God for granting him Ishmael and Isaac, a direct verbal answer to a gift received within a family.
God gives hearing, sight, and hearts to those born without knowledge so that they may be grateful, making human capacities gifts requiring thanks.
The prophets whom God favored fall prostrate and weeping when the signs are recited; the favored people answer with worship.
Israel's rescue from an enemy and the provision of manna and quails are presented together, concentrating several favors in one addressed community.
Hearing, sight, and hearts are given by God, followed by the rebuke that people are little grateful.
Moses addresses his Lord through the favor bestowed on him and turns it into a pledge not to support evildoers, an ethical use of received grace.
Those who had envied Qarun recognize after his fall that God graciously enlarges or restricts provision; the scene corrects ownership-like boasting over wealth.
Luqman is given wisdom and commanded to be grateful; the ayah says the grateful person's gratitude returns to himself, without enriching the Giver.
The garden-dwellers say that God favored and protected them from the fiery punishment, a remembered rescue at the end of the road.
Faithful hearers are promised two shares of mercy and a light by which to walk, joining given mercy to a traversable path.
Steadfastness on the path would bring abundant water; it makes the straight way a site where provision is given and tested.
Those who give wealth and do not follow it with mann or injury keep their reward. It is the Qur'anic boundary against the section's head-claimed favor.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury; giving that humiliates the receiver reverses the section's good passing from hand to hand.
Believers are forbidden to nullify charity through mann and injury, directly naming the destructive counterpart to unboastful goodness.
Those who love to be praised for what they did not do illuminate the section's secondary sense of hamd turned into a false claim rather than truthful acknowledgment.
Moses calls Pharaoh's claimed upbringing a favor that Pharaoh keeps holding over him, the precise dramatic scene of a benefaction turned into reproach.
Some treat their Islam as a favor conferred on the Prophet; the ayah reverses the direction, saying God favored them by guiding them to faith.
The command not to confer a favor while seeking more draws a boundary around giving: it must not become a means of extracting return or status.
The righteous give beloved food to the needy, orphan, and captive; their open hand contrasts with a gift retained as leverage.
They explicitly seek neither recompense nor thanks from those they feed, the inverse of giving in order to be praised or to remind the recipient.
Israel is asked how many clear signs it received, and changing God's favor after it arrives is set against faithful reception of a gift.
God does not change a favor He has bestowed until people change what is in themselves; favor has a moral boundary rather than automatic permanence.
People resent the Messenger even though God and His Messenger enriched them from bounty; it shows hostility answering a received good.
After receiving bounty, some become miserly and turn away, the receiver blocking the onward movement of a gift.
When mercy is removed after man tastes it, he despairs and becomes ungrateful; the ayah exposes a response that recognizes good only after losing it.
When favor follows adversity, man claims his troubles have gone and exults boastfully; the benefit becomes self-satisfaction instead of gratitude.
Those who exchange God's favor for disbelief make a named reversal of the section's praise-and-guidance response.
After God gives spouses, children, and good provision, people believe falsehood and deny God's favor; domestic abundance is met with denial.
People recognize God's favor and then deny it, the section's recipient refusing to name the actual giver.
A secure town with provision from every place denies God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear, reversing its received security.
When God bestows a favor on man, he turns away and distances himself; favor here produces withdrawal rather than praise.
The owner of a garden is asked why he did not acknowledge God's will and power upon entering it, correcting possession that speaks as if self-made.
When the garden's produce is destroyed, its owner wrings his hands over what he spent; the loss completes 18:39's warning about unacknowledged bounty.
After manna and quails, Israel is told not to transgress in the good things provided; provision has a boundary and does not license defiance.
A secure sanctuary with people snatched away around it is followed by the question whether they deny God's favor, making safety a favor that can be refused.
After people call on God in harm and He lets them taste mercy, a group associates partners; mercy is met with a false attribution.
Saba asks for longer distances between its safe, measured journeys and thereby wrongs itself; 34:18's blessed route is a favor the people reject.
When told to spend from what God has provided them, deniers refuse to feed those whom God could feed. It blocks the section's transfer of received good to another.
A person calls on his Lord in harm, then forgets that call once a favor is bestowed and assigns rivals to God; the favorable turn is not acknowledged.
After receiving a favor, a person says it came through his own knowledge; this self-attribution is a refined form of claiming the gift.
After mercy following harm, a person calls it his own and denies the Hour; the ayah contrasts a given mercy with possessive speech.
When God bestows a favor, man turns away; when harm touches him, he makes extended prayer. The two reactions reverse the section's proper order.
The owners of the garden plan that no needy person shall enter it, a narrative refusal to let a received harvest become goodness for another hand.
When his Lord tests him by generosity, man reads it as personal honor; the ayah separates a bestowed ease from self-flattering interpretation.
When provision is restricted, man calls it humiliation; together with 89:15 it rejects treating material allotment as a badge to claim.
Israel is told to remember God's favor and fulfill His covenant, making recollection of a benefit answerable in conduct.
Cloud shade, manna, and quails are given as good things for Israel to eat; the scene gives food directly to a people who must receive it rightly.
The command to turn toward the Sacred Mosque supplies the changed direction whose completion of favor and guidance are announced in 2:150.
Believers are told to remember God's favor and the Book and wisdom sent down to admonish them, treating teaching itself as received good.
Those who return unharmed do so with favor and bounty from God, showing protection after danger as a favor received rather than a personal triumph.
The community is told to remember God's favor and the covenant bound upon it, echoing 2:40's link between gift and faithful response.
God tells believers to remember His favor when He restrained hostile hands from them; the favor is a specific protection, not an abstraction.
Noah's people are told to remember God's favors after being made successors; a collective historical advantage is set before them as a call to heed.
Salih's people are told to remember God's favors after succession and settlement in the land; favor includes being made able to build and inhabit.
God reminds Israel that He favored them above the worlds, a collective form of the favored people named in Fatiha.
God joined believers' hearts where all earthly spending could not have done so; reconciliation becomes an unpurchasable good credited to its giver.
Those favored in provision do not share it equally with those under their authority, and the verse asks whether they deny God's favor; it challenges a recipient who withholds good.
God tells Moses that He had already bestowed favor on him another time, anchoring Moses's later mission in remembered grace.
After giving Zechariah John and restoring his wife, God describes the family as hastening to good works in hope and humility, a gift answered in conduct.
Animals provided for sacrifice may be eaten and fed to the contented and the needy; the gift is intentionally passed onward.
God distributes rain among people to remind them, yet most refuse anything but denial; a shared life-giving provision meets refusal.
Those with bounty are told not to withhold from relatives, needy people, and emigrants, but to pardon and overlook while hoping for God's forgiveness; received abundance is released as good.
Owners are told to give people seeking emancipation some of the wealth God has given them, making the giver's wealth explicitly a trust passed onward.
God declares His will to confer favor on the oppressed, make them leaders and inheritors, showing favor can lift an entire humiliated people.
Ships move by God's favor so that He may show signs to every patient, grateful person; travel itself exposes a favor to the grateful eye.
After forming people, God gives hearing, sight, and hearts and says they are little grateful, paralleling 16:78's gift and response.
Believers are told to remember God's favor when armies came against them and God sent wind and unseen forces, a concrete rescue in collective memory.
God places visible towns between Saba and blessed towns and measures safe journeys through them, making a traversable route itself a favor.
God says He bestowed favor upon Moses and Aaron, setting their prophetic deliverance among direct cases of divine benefaction.
A garden-dweller says that without his Lord's favor he would have been among those brought to punishment, naming rescue as unearned grace.
God calls Solomon's endowment a gift and permits him to give generously or withhold; a received divine gift is shown becoming power to dispense.
God forms people beautifully and provides good things, then is declared blessed as Lord of the worlds; provision turns into the language of praise.
Riders are taught to glorify the One who subjected transport to them, a spoken acknowledgment of a facility they could not master themselves.
The acknowledgment of subjected transport ends by recalling return to the Lord, preventing the journey's convenience from becoming self-sufficiency.
After the water questions of 56:68-69, God says He could make it brackish and asks why people are not grateful; drink becomes a test of thanks.
Fire is made a reminder and provision for travelers, identifying an ordinary aid as a supplied good.
After naming fire as provision, the ayah commands glorification of the great Lord, returning the useful gift to praise.
Water bursts from the rock for Israel and they are told to eat and drink from God's provision without spreading corruption; the gift carries a conduct-boundary.
God promises to reward the grateful, giving the section's gratitude an eschatological answer without reducing it to a transaction.
God asks why He would punish if people are grateful and believe, treating gratitude as a meaningful relation to mercy rather than empty speech.
At harvest people may eat the fruit but must give its due, turning received cultivation into provision for others.
Faith and reverence would open blessings from heaven and earth; the verse connects a community's way with an overflowing provision.
Moses is to remind his people of God's days, signs for every patient and grateful person; 14:6 makes one of those days a remembered rescue.
The Prophet's preserved revelation is described as mercy and a great favor from his Lord, treating guidance itself as an unearned endowment.
Job receives restored family and its like as mercy from God and a reminder for worshippers, so relief is explicitly tied to worship.
Pilgrims are to mention God's name over livestock He has provided, eat of it, and feed the distressed; recognition and redistribution meet in the rite.
The command to worship God and be among the grateful supplies the required stance of the recipient, even though no single material favor is named.
The subjection of all in the heavens and earth expands the sea-bounty of 45:12 into a comprehensive field for reflecting on received gifts.
What God grants as communal wealth is assigned to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so it does not merely circulate among the rich; received good is routed onward.
The Helpers give preference to emigrants even while needy themselves, showing a recipient of provision letting goodness reach another without self-assertion.
People are told to spend from what God has provided before death closes the chance, turning received provision into outward good.
The correction after claims of honor and humiliation is failure to honor the orphan, showing that wealth's proper test concerns what reaches the vulnerable.
Failure to urge feeding the poor continues 89:15-17's correction of possessive readings of provision; an alleged honor fails to become goodness for another.
Those who perform for show embody worship and giving directed toward human notice, the public-display opposite of the section's sincere hamd.
Withholding even small assistance completes 107:6's showy religion: the sought praise does not become actual good for another.

After God causes the fleeing multitude to die and restores them to life, the ayah calls Him full of bounty toward people while most do not give thanks; revived life is a concrete favor with a failed response.
God's favor and mercy protect the Prophet from a plot, and His Book, wisdom, and teaching are named as part of that great favor; guidance arrives as undeserved preservation.
Some speak contemptuously of those whom God has favored among them, while the ayah closes by naming God as knowing the grateful; social scorn reverses recognition of recipients of favor.
After God gives a sound child, the recipients associate partners with Him in what He gave them; a particular family gift is met with false attribution.
Some criticize the distribution of alms: they are satisfied when given from it and angry when withheld. The verse shows a recipient treating a gift as an entitlement.
The corrective response to alms distribution is contentment with what God and His Messenger gave, saying God is sufficient, and hoping for His bounty rather than resentful demand.
God honors the children of Adam, carries them on land and sea, provides good things, and favors them over much creation; transport and provision form a broad concrete favor scene.
The ayah says that without God's favor and mercy none would ever be purified, making mercy the source that repairs and completes people rather than a benefit they possess.
After recalling a mother's hardship in bearing and weaning, God commands gratitude to Himself and to parents; received care is answered both upward and within the human chain.
Whatever people spend, God promises to replace it; the section's movement of goodness outward is joined to the Giver's replenishing increase.
God makes faith beloved, adorns it in believers' hearts, and calls this bounty and favor from Him; the favor is specifically an inward guidance that shapes a path.
After people taste mercy following harm, they scheme against God's signs; the ayah gives a distinct post-relief reversal rather than gratitude.
In danger at sea people call on God alone, but after He delivers them to land they turn away; rescue is followed by refusal to acknowledge its giver.
When people taste mercy they rejoice, but when harm comes through their own hands the human being is called ungrateful; the ayah makes unstable reception of mercy a named contrast.
God pardons Israel after the calf episode so that they may give thanks, making forgiveness a mercy that calls for the same responsive acknowledgment as material favor.
A goodly loan to God is promised multiplication and forgiveness; giving becomes a scene of added return, resonating with the section's dictionary sense of giving more.
Both the affluent and the constrained are told to spend from what God has given them, treating provision as something received that should reach beyond its holder.
Noah's call to seek forgiveness is followed by promised rain and abundance in 71:12; repentance opens the way to mercy and provision.
The promised result is rain, wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, a concentrated scene of provision following 71:10's return to the forgiving Lord.
